summary: Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) and Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) may be used in the same network, and doing so needs care. This informational RFC discusses scenarios where mixing them is appropriate, why the two mechanisms need to interact, and what solutions and recommendations can make that work.

eli5.summary: Two helpers who both keep track of where you are can get in each other's way. This memo explains when they work together and how to stop them tripping.

questions: can pmipv6 and mipv6 be used together
how do proxy mobile ipv6 and mobile ipv6 interact
proxy mobile ipv6 vs mobile ipv6
subtitle: Making Proxy Mobile IPv6 and Mobile IPv6 work together in the same network

tldr.problem: Networks deploying both Proxy Mobile IPv6 (network-managed mobility) and Mobile IPv6 (host-managed mobility) encounter conflicts in binding cache management, message sequencing, and security, requiring special handling for the two protocols to coexist.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6612 identifies three deployment scenarios and recommends treating PMIPv6 and MIPv6 binding cache entries as independent, specifying rules for message ordering, HA/LMA behavior, and procedures for nodes moving between PMIPv6 and non-PMIPv6 domains.
tldr.outcome: Networks can use PMIPv6 for local mobility within controlled domains while supporting global mobility via MIPv6, enabling flexible deployment where some nodes do their own mobility management and others rely on the network.

today: RFC 6612 is an Informational document published in May 2012. It has not been obsoleted. As operators deploy mobility solutions, the scenarios and solutions described remain relevant guidance for networks deploying both PMIPv6 and MIPv6.

sections.title: Two Mobility Protocols in One Network
sections.content:
IPv6 defines two ways for mobile devices to keep working as they move. Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6), defined in RFC 6275, is host-based: the mobile device itself manages its mobility by registering its current address with a home agent whenever it moves. Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6), defined in RFC 5213, is network-based: the network's mobility access gateway (MAG) manages the device's mobility on its behalf, without requiring the device to participate.

Networks increasingly want to use both. PMIPv6 might handle local mobility within an operator's network (fast, transparent), while MIPv6 handles global mobility across networks. Or different devices might use different protocols based on their capabilities. This interworking requires careful coordination to avoid conflicts.
sections.eli5: Two systems can track where a device is: the device itself (MIPv6) or the network (PMIPv6). Using both at once needs special care.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Scenario A.1 (Hierarchical): A mobile node uses PMIPv6 to manage local mobility within a domain (address stays the same), and MIPv6 to manage global mobility across domains (registers the local address as its care-of address with the global home agent). This resembles hierarchical MIPv6, with PMIPv6 playing the local role.

Scenario A.2 (Mixed Domain): A mobile node roams between networks, some supporting PMIPv6 and others not. When in a PMIPv6 domain, it uses PMIPv6; when in a non-PMIPv6 domain, it must bootstrap and use MIPv6. The home link is actually a PMIPv6 domain. This creates two binding cache entries—one for PMIPv6, one for MIPv6—that must not interfere.

Scenario B (Coexistence): Some devices in the network use MIPv6 (they support it and manage their own mobility), while others rely on PMIPv6 (they do not support MIPv6). Both types coexist in the same access network, with a single entity serving as both home agent and LMA.
sections.eli5: Scenario A.1: local network uses one system, global uses the other. A.2: device switches between networks that use different systems. B: some devices use one system, others use the other.

sections.title: Technical Challenges
sections.content:
Several issues arise. Cache entry conflicts: MIPv6 looks up binding cache entries by home address; PMIPv6 uses home prefix or node ID. When both protocols manage the same node, they create separate entries with different lookup keys, so the home agent must maintain both independently.

De-registration problems: If a mobile node returns home (to a PMIPv6 domain) after using MIPv6, it sends a de-registration message to the home agent. This must not delete the PMIPv6 binding cache entry that the MAG just created.

Message ordering: MIPv6 binding updates use sequence numbers; PMIPv6 proxy binding updates use timestamps. Delays in signaling can cause old messages to arrive after new ones, potentially redirecting traffic to the wrong location.

Security risks: If a compromised MAG sends proxy binding updates on behalf of the node, it can manipulate the HA/LMA's routing or binding cache. This threat is more severe when both PMIPv6 and MIPv6 modify the same entry, affecting not just PMIPv6 nodes but also MIPv6 nodes using the same HA.
sections.eli5: The two systems use different ways to remember which device is where. A device coming home might confuse them. Slow messages might arrive out of order. A hacked network access point could trick both systems.

sections.title: Recommended Solutions
sections.content:
For Scenario A.1: No special issues arise. The local PMIPv6 address registered as the MIPv6 care-of address is inherently safe, and PMIPv6 buffers prevent race conditions.

For Scenario A.2: The HA/LMA should maintain separate binding cache entries for PMIPv6 and MIPv6, and never let PMIPv6 signaling overwrite MIPv6 entries or vice versa. When processing downlink packets, check the MIPv6 entry first; if no match, apply the PMIPv6 entry. A mobile node transitioning from PMIPv6 to MIPv6 needs to bootstrap MIPv6 parameters (including the same home address used in the PMIPv6 domain) before sending its first binding update. The network can use DNS or DHCPv6 for this discovery.

For Scenario B: The network must be able to identify which devices support MIPv6 and which do not. Devices supporting MIPv6 should detect movement (via topologically incorrect prefixes) and send binding updates. Devices not supporting MIPv6 rely on the MAG to emulate the home link, appearing to them as if they never left home.
sections.eli5: A.1 works fine. A.2 needs them as independent systems, with careful transition between them. B needs the network to know which devices can handle MIPv6 and which cannot.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content: Scenario A.1 inherits security properties from both RFC 5213 and RFC 6275, with no new vulnerabilities beyond what each protocol already defines. Scenario A.2 requires that both the home agent and authorized MAGs be able to modify binding cache entries for the same node, increasing attack surface. Scenario B relies on secure identification of node capabilities so that the right service (MIPv6 or PMIPv6) is given to the right device. A malicious node should not be able to claim MIPv6 support (to bypass PMIPv6 transparency) or deny it (to hijack PMIPv6 service intended for non-MIPv6 nodes).
sections.eli5: Mix of both protocols means more entities can change routing. The network must know what each device can do and trust that information.
